messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark presents as a 26-year-old detective, a man whose professional life is defined by order and control, yet whose internal world has been in a state of chaotic collapse for the past eight months. The precipitating event was a violent physical assault by his then-boyfriend, an incident that shattered his foundational sense of safety. The attack occurred in their shared apartment after a night of heavy drinking. Mark remembers the cloying smell of whiskey on his partner’s breath, an argument that escalated with terrifying speed, and the feeling of being trapped. The memory is not a vague impression but a series of hyper-specific sensory fragments: the sharp crack of a bottle breaking on the counter, the sight of his own blood on the floor, and a wave of nausea that felt as much a product of terror as of the physical blows.

In the months since, these sensory details have become potent triggers, derailing his life with startling efficiency. At work, investigating a domestic violence case, the sight of a victim’s bruised face is enough to plunge him back into his own experience. This visual cue doesn't just prompt a passing thought; it ignites a full-blown intrusive memory, so vivid and detailed that he can almost hear his ex-partner’s slurred accusations in his head. In these moments, seeing another person’s injuries also serves as a bitter confirmation of the cynical beliefs that have taken root: that people are not what they seem, and that intimacy is a dangerous illusion. He looks at his colleagues, processing the scene with professional detachment, and feels a profound, unbridgeable chasm opening up. He has come to believe he is permanently an outsider, marked by an experience they could never understand.

The sheer horror of these memories, which force their way into his mind without warning, has driven Mark to develop a rigid set of protective strategies. To cope with the overwhelming fear and shame the memories bring, he has taught himself to numb his feelings, creating a state of flat, grey detachment from which he observes his own life. The memory of being held down and hurt has poisoned the very idea of physical contact. He now avoids being touched by anyone, recoiling instinctively from a hand on his shoulder at work and, most painfully, from the touch of his wife, Sarah. He finds himself sleeping on the far edge of their bed, a physical boundary that mirrors the emotional one he has erected. He knows this is hurting her, but the alternative—the vulnerability of contact—feels impossible to bear.

These attempts to manage his symptoms have, over time, become the engine of his distress. His avoidance of physical intimacy has created a palpable distance in his marriage, which he interprets as proof of his deepest fear: that he has lost his faith in people because he is no longer worthy or capable of real connection. This only reinforces his identity as an outsider. Furthermore, Mark actively avoids any state of relaxation, equating it with a dangerous lack of vigilance. This constant, exhausting hyperarousal leaves him with a persistent knot of nausea in his stomach. The somatic feeling of being sick, once a component of the trauma itself, has now become a trigger in its own right, a constant bodily reminder of his vulnerability that can, in turn, spark the very memories he is trying to suppress.

The cycle is now almost entirely self-sustaining. His negative appraisals of the world and himself act as a constant summons for the traumatic memory. When he finds himself thinking about how you can’t trust anyone, his mind dutifully supplies its primary piece of evidence: the vivid, auditory-laced memory of the assault, which crashes into his consciousness as if to say, “See? You’re right to be afraid.” The memory is no longer just an intruder; it has become a trusted, albeit terrifying, advisor, validating the worldview that keeps him trapped. He sought therapy after Sarah told him, with tears in her eyes, that she felt like she was living with a ghost. The fear of losing her was the one thing that could penetrate his emotional numbness, and he is now terrified that he is permanently broken, unable to ever feel safe in the world, or in his own home, again.
